quote: Einstein generated the theory of Special Relativity using Mach’s Principle, which is the physicist’s version of the Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle.
content: Mach’s principle, the proposal that inertia arises from the distribution of distant matter, had nothing to do with special relativity and was named by Einstein in 1918 as an aspiration for the general theory, one he later abandoned. The 1905 paper opens with the asymmetry in the electrodynamics of a moving magnet and conductor, invokes the principle of relativity (Galileo’s, extended to electromagnetism) and the constancy of the speed of light, and derives the Lorentz transformations; its influences were Maxwell, Lorentz, Poincaré and, in a general philosophical way, Mach’s and Hume’s scepticism about absolute concepts, which is not Mach’s principle. The essay’s gloss, that an unobservable absolute speed “shouldn’t ought to exist,” is a verificationist reading of the relativity principle that the annotations on Book II found the book disowning elsewhere. The comparison to the Generalized Anti-Zombie Principle is also inexact in the other direction: relativity says the absolute frame is undetectable and therefore drops it from the theory; the anti-zombie principle says consciousness is detectable through its effects and therefore keeps it. The two principles run opposite ways.

quote: When Einstein invented General Relativity, he had almost no experimental data to go on, except the precession of Mercury’s perihelion. And (as far as I know) Einstein did not use that data, except at the end.
content: He used it in the middle, and it told him he was wrong. In 1913 Einstein and Besso computed Mercury’s perihelion advance from the Entwurf theory, the non-covariant field equations Einstein then held, and got about 18 arcseconds against the observed 43; the manuscript survives. He defended the Entwurf theory for two more years with the “hole argument,” abandoned it in the autumn of 1915, and in November obtained the correct 43″ from the new equations, an outcome he described as giving him palpitations and which was the decisive check that convinced him the equations were right (Norton (1984); Janssen and Renn, “Untying the Knot,” in The Genesis of General Relativity, 2007). Book I’s annotations on Einstein’s Arrogance recorded the same history. So “the whole long (multi-year!) chain of armchair reasoning, without making any mistakes that would have required further experimental evidence to pull him back on track” describes a chain that contained a mistaken theory held for two years and a piece of experimental evidence that helped pull him off it. The equivalence principle from which the chain starts is itself an empirical fact, the equality of inertial and gravitational mass, measured by Eötvös to a part in a hundred million. The essay wants Einstein as the demonstration that armchair reasoning can win; the record is that armchair reasoning plus Mercury won, after armchair reasoning alone had lost.

quote: Asked what he would have done if Eddington’s solar eclipse observation had failed to confirm General Relativity, Einstein replied: “Then I would feel sorry for the good Lord. The theory is correct.”
content: Book I’s annotations traced this: it comes from Ilse Rosenthal-Schneider’s recollection, published decades later, of a remark made after the result was known, not before. The parenthesis that follows, that the 1919 measurement “had favored General Relativity essentially by luck,” repeats Earman and Glymour’s 1980 reanalysis, which has since been reassessed: Kennefick’s re-examination of the plates and the reduction procedures found Eddington’s treatment of the Sobral astrographic data defensible on grounds available at the time (Kennefick (2009)), and a 1979 remeasurement of the original plates with modern methods confirmed the relativistic value. The essay corrects the popular story with an older revisionist story that has itself been revised. The larger point survives either way: Science did wait for the eclipse, and it was right to, since the prediction of light deflection was the theory’s first genuinely novel one.

quote: The most sane thinking I have seen in any scientific field comes from the field of evolutionary psychology, possibly because they understand self-deception, but also perhaps because they often (1) have to reason from scanty evidence and (2) do later find out if they were right or wrong.
content: The field the essay nominates as the model of careful reasoning on scanty evidence is the field whose reasoning on scanty evidence came out worst when checked. Book III’s annotations went through the record: the Ekman universals, the mate-preference surveys against revealed preference, the ovulatory-cycle effects, the thrifty gene, the willpower stories, the grief correlation, in each case a satisfying ancestral story supported by a small sample from a WEIRD population that did not replicate or did not generalize. The essay’s criterion (2), that practitioners later find out if they were right, is exactly the criterion the field failed, since its central claims were about a Pleistocene environment no one can observe and its testable claims were tested badly. Tooby and Cosmides’s “The Psychological Foundations of Culture” (1992), the recommended text, is a programmatic manifesto with no data of its own. It is possible that the essay’s author was seeing careful reasoning in the field’s best practitioners; the field, as a whole, is the cautionary example for the method this essay recommends.
